extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners and parties in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) inter partes proceedings (trademark attorneys, in-house counsel, litigants)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural and substantive standards for discovery in TTAB inter partes trademark proceedings, focusing on interrogatories and requests for production (including ESI): when discovery is permitted, scope, numerical limits and counting rules, timing and form of responses, signature/authority requirements, and remedies for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When permitted to serve interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, a party may serve written interrogatories on any other party during the discovery period only if the serving party previously served or concurrently serves therewith its initial disclosures, absent a stipulation or a granted motion, or upon order of the Board to the contrary. Interrogatories may be served from the opening of the discovery period through the last day of the discovery period. Interrogatories may not be served on a non-party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See TBMP § 403.01 and § 403.02; notes cite 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 33. Parties may serve interrogatories up to the last day of discovery even if answers will be due after the discovery period closes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatories may seek any information that is discoverable under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b). An interrogatory that is otherwise proper is not necessarily objectionable merely because it requires a party to give an opinion or contention that relates to fact or the application of law to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a)(2) and case law (e.g., Johnston Pump/General Valve Inc. v. Chromalloy) that a query requiring a legal conclusion may still be answerable. See TBMP § 402 for scope discussion under Rule 26(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical limit on interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: The total number of written interrogatories which a party may serve upon another party in a proceeding shall not exceed seventy-five, counting subparts, except that the Board may allow additional interrogatories upon motion showing good cause, or upon stipulation of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion for leave to serve additional interrogatories must be filed and granted prior to service of the additional interrogatories and must be accompanied by copies of interrogatories already served and proposed additional interrogatories. See 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit applies to entire proceeding (sets combined)
rubrics_metrics.description: The numerical limit pertains to the total number of interrogatories that one party may serve on another over the course of an entire proceeding, not per set of interrogatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple sets are served over time, the interrogatories in the separate sets are added together for the 75-count limit. Parties preparing the first set should reserve part of the allotted 75 for follow-up discovery. (See Baron Phillippe De Rothschild S.A. v. S. Rothschild & Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No automatic extra interrogatories for multiple marks or counterclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1) does not provide for extra interrogatories where more than one mark is pleaded/attacked or where there is a counterclaim; the propounding party may request that each interrogatory be answered with respect to each involved mark, and the interrogatories will be counted the same as if they pertained to only one mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple marks and/or counterclaims are not in themselves good cause for additional interrogatories, though unusually numerous or complex issues may be considered in deciding motions to permit additional interrogatories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting interrogatories and subparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Each subpart within an interrogatory is counted as a separate interrogatory, regardless of whether the subpart is separately designated. If more than 75 questions are contained despite numbering, the Board will look to substance and count each question. Compound questions, conditional follow-ups, broad introductory clauses plus subparts, and requests seeking information on multiple issues will be counted as separate interrogatories as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: separately designated subparts count separately; combining multiple questions in one compound interrogatory will be parsed by substance; an initial question plus each conditional follow-up are separate; broad introductory clause and each subpart are counted. Conversely, an interrogatory seeking 'all relevant facts and circumstances' concerning a single issue may be counted as a single interrogatory. The introductory preamble is not counted. (Cites Jan Bell Marketing, Kellogg, Pyttronic, and Notice of Final Rulemaking.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy and procedure for excessive interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party believes the number of interrogatories served exceeds the numerical limit, it must, within the time for (and instead of) serving answers and specific objections, serve a general objection on the ground of excessive number. If the propounding party files a motion to compel, the motion must be accompanied by copies of the set(s) said to exceed the limitation and must comply with 37 CFR § 2.120(e), including a written statement that the moving party made a good faith effort to resolve the issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is improper to answer what one believes are the first 75 and object to the rest. The moving party should set out its counting method. If the Board finds interrogatories excessive and the propounding party has not used up its allotted 75, the Board normally will allow a revised set not exceeding the limit; the revised set is deemed timely if the excessive set was timely but may not seek broader scope if served after discovery closes. Parties are encouraged to agree voluntarily to a revised set rather than litigate. A party may refuse to respond to document requests seeking documents identified in answers if the number of interrogatories is believed excessive. (Cites 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1)-(e), TBMP § 523, and cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for service of responses to interrogatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to interrogatories must be served within 30 days after the date of service of the interrogatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If service is by first-class mail, Express Mail, or overnight courier, the date of mailing or delivery to courier is service date and five extra days are allowed for responding. If parties agree to electronic service (fax/email), no additional time is allowed. Failure to respond within allowed time, absent excusable neglect, may result in forfeiture of the right to object to interrogatories on their merits. (Cites 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3), Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(2), TBMP §§ 403.03, 113.05.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and scope of objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections going to the merits of an interrogatory include irrelevance, over-breadth, vagueness, burdensomeness, or not likely to lead to admissible evidence. Objections based on privilege or attorney work product go to a characteristic of the information and generally will not be found waived by late responses. Objections based on confidentiality are expected to be extremely limited because the Board's standard protective order is in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party that fails to respond and can't show excusable neglect may forfeit the right to object on the merits. See relevant TTAB cases (No Fear Inc. v. Rule; Envirotech; Crane Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Answering each interrogatory and option to produce business records (Rule 33(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Each interrogatory must, to the extent not objected to, be answered separately and fully in writing under oath. Alternatively, if the answer may be determined by examining business records and the burden of deriving the answer is substantially the same for either party, the responding party may (1) specify the records in sufficient detail to enable the interrogating party to locate and identify them as readily as the responding party could, and (2) give a reasonable opportunity to examine, audit, or copy the records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the responding party elects to answer by specifying business records, the specification must be sufficiently detailed. A party invoking Rule 33(d) with regard to electronic information may be required to provide technical support or information on application software. If direct access to an electronic system is necessary, privacy/confidentiality concerns may justify deriving the answer without granting access. A responding party cannot simultaneously invoke Rule 33(d) and claim privilege as to the same documents. Case law sets out prerequisites for invoking this option (e.g., Johnson & Johnson v. WDS; Jain v. Ramparts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and content of interrogatory responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily a responding party should reproduce each interrogatory immediately preceding the answer or objection. If an interrogatory is answered, the answer must be made separately and fully in writing under oath. If objected to, the specific reasons for objection must be stated in lieu of an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is generally inappropriate to respond by filing motions attacking the interrogatories (strike, suppress, protective order); instead respond to proper interrogatories and state specific objections to improper ones. See TBMP § 410. See also TBMP § 408.03 for duty to supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature and authority of respondent and signer
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogatories must be answered by the party to whom they are directed, or if that party is a corporation/partnership/association/governmental agency, by any officer or agent who must furnish the information available to the party. The person who makes the answers must sign them, and the attorney who objects must sign any objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'agent' includes an attorney, who may answer even without personal knowledge; however, attorney answers may expose the attorney to additional discovery and possibly disqualification. (Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(1),(5) and TTAB decisions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When permitted to serve requests for production (documents/ESI)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inter partes proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, a party may serve requests for production of documents and things (including ESI) on any other party only during the discovery period and provided the serving party has previously served or is serving concurrently its initial disclosures, absent stipulation, granted motion, or Board order. Requests for production may be served through the last day of the discovery period, though responses may be due after the period closes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If document requests are combined with a notice of taking a discovery deposition, special timing (e.g., at least 35 days prior if served by mail) applies. Requests for production may not be served on a non-party (but production from a nonparty deponent may be obtained by subpoena duces tecum or voluntarily). See TBMP § 113.04-.05 and § 403.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-law considerations for document production
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties seeking production from a natural person residing in a foreign country should be aware that foreign laws may preclude such discovery. In determining whether to impose sanctions for non-compliance due to foreign law conflict, the Board considers (1) the good faith of the non-complying party; (2) whether the non-complying party would incur foreign criminal liability; and (3) whether alternative sources of information are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Societe Internationale v. Rogers and Cochran Consulting v. Uwatec and notes potential limitations when foreign legal prohibitions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of requests for production (what may be requested)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may request production of any designated documents or ESI (writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, sound recordings, images, and other data or data compilations) stored in any medium from which information can be obtained, or designated tangible things, or entry onto designated property for inspection — subject to Rule 26(b) scope limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, a party is not obligated to locate documents not in its possession, custody, or control, nor to create documents that do not exist; but a party may not mislead its adversary by promising production and then claiming no possession or control. Because TTAB proceedings concern registration rights, entry onto land is rarely used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements required in a request for production
rubrics_metrics.description: A request must (A) describe with reasonable particularity each item or category to be inspected; (B) specify a reasonable time, place, and manner for inspection and related acts; and (C) may specify the form(s) in which ESI is to be produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are expected to discuss ESI production formats during the mandatory discovery conference. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(1) and TBMP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses to requests for production — timing and required content
rubrics_metrics.description: The party to whom a request is directed must respond in writing within 30 days after being served. For each item or category, the response must either state that inspection and related activities will be permitted as requested or state an objection to the request, including the reasons. An objection to part of a request must specify the part and permit inspection of the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special ESI rules: the response may object to a requested form for producing ESI — if the responding party objects or no form is specified, the party must state the form(s) it intends to use. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2). Mailing and electronic service timing rules as for interrogatories apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production format and organization of produced documents/ESI
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless stipulated or ordered, a party must produce documents as they are kept in the usual course of business or must organize and label them to correspond to the categories in the request. If a request does not specify a form for producing ESI, a party must produce it in a form or forms in which it is ordinarily maintained or in a reasonably usable form or forms. A party need not produce the same ESI in more than one form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents produced in ESI form not kept in the ordinary course must be organized and labeled to correspond to request categories (example: for large DVD productions, opposer ordered to serve complete index cross-referencing categories with page limits per category). See Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(E) and Amazon Technologies v. Wax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time for service of responses to requests for production (reinforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to requests for production must be served within 30 days after service of the requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(b)(2)(A) and TBMP § 403.03; timing nuances regarding mail/courier/electronic service described above.
